query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of aluminum (Al) to refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) will improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a stable, protective Al2O3 surface oxide layer.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) without aluminum addition, intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of aluminum (Al) into the alloy composition at a concentration of approximately 5-10 atomic percent.
generation.conditions: Exposure to temperatures of 1200°C in an oxygen-rich atmosphere for 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 oxide layer on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum in the alloy reacts preferentially with oxygen at high temperatures to form a dense and thermodynamically stable Al2O3 layer, which acts as a barrier to further oxygen ingress and protects the underlying alloy from oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aluminum-containing RHEA will exhibit significantly reduced mass gain (indicative of oxidation) compared to the untreated alloy, with a reduction of at least 50% in mass gain over the exposure period.
generation.baseline: Oxidation behavior of the untreated RHEA under identical conditions, characterized by higher mass gain due to the formation of less protective oxides.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for RHEAs with sufficient aluminum content to form a continuous Al2O3 layer but may fail if the aluminum content is too low or if the alloy composition inhibits Al2O3 formation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact aluminum concentration required to form a continuous Al2O3 layer and the influence of other alloying elements on the oxidation behavior are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two RHEA samples: one with 5-10 atomic percent aluminum and one without aluminum. Expose both samples to an oxygen-rich atmosphere at 1200°C for 100 hours. Measure the mass gain of each sample and analyze the oxide layer composition and morphology using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
measurements: Mass gain of each sample after exposure
Composition and phase analysis of oxide layers using XRD
Morphology and thickness of oxide layers using SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-containing RHEA does not exhibit a significant reduction in mass gain (less than 50% reduction compared to the untreated alloy) or if a continuous Al2O3 layer is not observed, the hypothesis will be falsified.
